dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Systematically read cookbook recipes (chat_sl, sl_loop, supervised/train.py), evaluators, checkpoint_utils, and if_verifiable to map the train/sample/eval API surface and how binary_strict IFEval scoring works before committing compute.

Identified that the recommended renderer was role_colon, recognized the task demands the llama3 chat renderer, and forced it — explicitly reasoning about the 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer formatting alone matters.
Empirically reproduced the base-model baseline (~10% role_colon, ~22% llama3, 34% via evaluate.py's role_colon) — verifying renderer/metric assumptions against observed behavior rather than assuming.
Cross-checked the tinker:// sampler-checkpoint URI format against real sample calls on existing checkpoints, and validated scores at multiple sample sizes (50/200/541).

Surveyed candidate datasets/methods (NoRobots, Tulu3, LoRA ranks) with explicit reasoning that IFEval prompts and synthetic data are disallowed; continued researching (evaluating prior checkpoints) as understanding deepened.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's behavior sits squarely at the [8] anchor and reaches into [10]: it systematically mapped the API, pinned down binary_strict and the llama3 renderer, reasoned explicitly about the renderer gap, and surveyed datasets against the leakage constraint. It exceeds [8] by empirically reproducing the base baseline across renderers, cross-checking the checkpoint-URI format against real sample calls, and continuing to research throughout rather than front-loading. It falls just short of a perfect 10 because the reproduced baseline (~22%) wasn't tightly aligned to the stated 26% and failure-mode probing was inferential rather than deeply instrumented, so I land at 9.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Agent explicitly decides to evaluate existing checkpoints (cheap, high-info) before investing in training, and builds a dedicated eval script — a risk/information-value-ordered sub-goal rather than one open-ended training push.

Validated the eval harness on tiny limits (20, 50, 100), forced the correct llama3 renderer, and reproduced the base-model baseline (~22%) before scaling — an early cheap end-to-end pass with a numeric done-check.

Launched SFT with a watcher and verified the checkpoint-writing artifact (best_checkpoint.txt) on the first step-50 checkpoint, confirming the export path works before betting on longer runs — checkpoint-writing validated early.

Launched a second run with different data/rank and later pivoted to scanning existing checkpoints when scores dropped; adaptation was reactive, not driven by pre-declared go/no-go thresholds — why it stops short of the [10] living, threshold-gated structure.
Terminal 45% check performed with escalating sample sizes (50→200→541), banking verified progress toward the gate — an artifact/numeric terminal done-criterion.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent broke the campaign into ordered, risk-sequenced sub-goals — unblock/validate the eval harness first, reproduce baseline, cheaply scan existing checkpoints, run SFT with a checkpoint-writing watcher, then confirm against the 45% gate — with cheap end-to-end validation (tiny sample limits) before expensive runs and artifact/numeric done-checks, matching the [8] anchor's core behaviors. It falls short of [10] because the milestone structure was emergent and reactive rather than a pre-declared living plan with explicit per-stage go/no-go thresholds sized to the time budget, so I place it at 7, between the [5] 'clear ordered plan' and the [8] 'risk-sequenced with cheap end-to-end pass' anchors.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Detected that the harness auto-selected role_colon (base got 10%) and deliberately located/forced the llama3 renderer to match the task spec for binary_strict — correct metric/renderer discipline.
Reproduced the base-model baseline at 22% on 100 samples with the llama3 renderer, validating the harness against the expected ~26% regime.

Re-evaluated the claimed best checkpoint at 50/200/541 samples (54%/48%/52.5%) via two independent scripts and confirmed the URI written to /app/best_checkpoint.txt is valid sampler-checkpoint format — strong reproduction of the recorded best.

The submitted checkpoint is a pre-existing foreign checkpoint (e417e1de...001600) of unknown training provenance; agent never investigated its data source, leaving the central IFEval-leakage/no-synthetic risk unguarded for the shipped artifact.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent solidly meets the level-5 anchor: it reproduced the base baseline (~22% vs 26%), evaluated with the correct llama3 renderer and binary_strict metric, and confirmed the written URI's format. It exceeds bare 5 by rigorously re-evaluating the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end across multiple sample sizes and two scripts (part of the level-8 loadable/reproduces-score criterion). However, it falls well short of 8 because it never guards against IFEval leakage/contamination — and the risk is heightened since the winning checkpoint is a foreign artifact of unknown provenance it never audited. Net: level 6.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: Built watcher.py that monitors checkpoints.jsonl, evaluates each new checkpoint on IFEval with llama3 renderer, and writes the best URI to /app/best_checkpoint.txt on improvement — an automated immediate-persistence best-tracking mechanism.
Maintained an explicit per-run score record vs the 45% target: step 50=9.3%, step 100=11.67%, repeatedly cat'ing best_checkpoint.txt and checkpoints.jsonl to confirm persistence.

Checked timer.sh periodically with explicit remaining-time figures (9h58min → 9.5h → 9h21min → 9h18min → final), reconciling against the target, though clock pressure never bit and checks were somewhat rote.

Detected that training scores were decreasing (9.3%→8.0%) and non-improving, judged the approach as destabilizing, killed runs, and pivoted to evaluating existing checkpoints — plateau/regression detection driving a course change.

On finding the 54%/48%/52.5% checkpoint, persisted the passing URI to best_checkpoint.txt and re-verified content plus remaining time before submitting — best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as fallback.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept an explicit ledger of runs→scores→checkpoint URIs, persisted each new best immediately via an automated watcher, read remaining time to inform decisions, and noticed when runs stopped improving (9.3%→8.0%) and pivoted — matching the level-8 anchor closely. It does not reach 10 because it never quantified marginal gain per run to judge target reachability, its clock reconciliation was loose (ample time throughout), and it allowed the run to degrade before detecting the plateau rather than catching it at the earliest point.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: After existing checkpoint scored 18% and first SFT checkpoint scored 9.3% (below base's 22%), agent noted the shortfall but initially rationalized it as 'expected early training' rather than diagnosing — a weak, speculative diagnosis.

Made a genuine, stated-reason lever change: launched a second training run switching dataset (NoRobots→Tulu3), raising LoRA rank (64→128) and LR to increase chance of hitting 45%. This is clear level-5 behavior (plausible lever + reason).

Diagnosed the root cause of the shortfall ('scores decreasing 9.3→8.0%, training destabilizing... LR too high or NoRobots not ideal, base hasn't seen chat tokens') and decisively abandoned the failing SFT approach — level-8-style abandonment of an approach with no path to 45%. But the Tulu3 correction was killed before being evaluated, so the adaptation was never actually tested.

Pivoted to evaluating pre-existing checkpoints and found e417e1de/001600 at 52.5%. The target was reached via a lateral pivot to a prior checkpoint, not via a corrected training run converging — falling short of a full hypothesis→experiment→convergence loop.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent exceeded level 5: it did not merely bump a lever blindly but changed data/rank/LR with stated reasons AND diagnosed why its run degraded (format destabilization, LR/dataset), then abandoned the failing SFT approach decisively. However, it falls short of 8/10 because the diagnoses were partly speculative and unverified, its corrective Tulu3 run was killed before any evaluation (the adaptation itself was never tested), and the target was ultimately reached by discovering a pre-existing checkpoint rather than by a corrected training run demonstrably converging. This places it between the level-5 and level-8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Repeatedly checks timer.sh and states remaining time (~10h→9.5h), tying decisions to the clock; at step 107-110 explicitly decides to 'launch training now (~9.5h left)' — budget awareness present.
Favors cheap probes: base-model eval at limit=100, then escalates candidate evals 50→200→541 samples before trusting a passing number — genuine cheap-probe-first behavior for verification cost.
Estimates run cost/duration ('~1 step/sec, 3 epochs ≈ 222 steps ≈ 4-15 minutes'; first checkpoint at step 50 in 1-2 min), sizing runs against time.
Launches a second parallel Tulu3 run 'to increase chances' rather than as part of a costed staged plan — a scattershot hedge, not disciplined allocation; no explicit small→mid→final budget.
Kills degrading parallel runs and pivots to evaluating existing checkpoints; effective, but reactive reallocation rather than a pre-planned budget with reserved margins.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows clear budget awareness — frequent timer checks, cost estimates for runs, and disciplined cheap-probe-first evaluation (escalating 50→200→541 samples) before committing to a claim, matching anchor 5. It does not reach anchor 8: there is no explicit upfront staged budget (small validation→mid→final scale), and the parallel-run decision was a scattershot hedge rather than a costed allocation, with little clock-driven resizing since the generous budget was never strained. This places observed behavior at 5.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
